judge_assessment.explanation: I checked the judge's central claim -- that it 'mapped the angle labels' and that the diagram is consistent with every named relationship -- by reconstructing the figure from worksheet.tex rather than from the caption. Line l is y=1, line m is y=-1, and transversal t runs along y=x, so t meets l at (1,1) and m at (-1,-1); the eight label coordinates put a in the upper-right sector at l, b upper-left, c lower-left, d lower-right, and e/f/g/h in the same four positions at m. That fixes the corresponding pairs as (a,e), (b,f), (c,g), (d,h), and every relationship the sheet asserts follows: a and d are a linear pair (they share the ray of l to the right of t and their other sides are opposite rays of t), so 180-118=62 and e=118 in problem 1; c and f are same-side interior, so 133 and g=47 in problem 2; b and f correspond, so 3x+10=5x-24 gives x=17 and 61; b and h are alternate exterior (125) with h and e a linear pair (55); d and f alternate interior, so x=12 and 69, and 108 then 72 via the linear pair a-d; c and f same-side interior, so 10x+20=180, x=16 and 76; d and e same-side interior, so 8x+4=180, x=22 and 102; a and g alternate exterior, so x=15 and 64; and in problem 10 b and e are supplementary via b-corresponds-to-f then f-e linear pair, giving 12x+12=180, x=14 and 122 (check 122+58=180). Every value the judge lists is right, the single manual item it counted matches verify.json id 10, and the study guide's six pairings and four try-its (68/112, x=15/55, x=9/47, x=21/115, x=14/102) all check out. I found no defect to add.

strengths_to_preserve: Problem 10 chooses a pair with NO single standard name (b exterior at l, e interior at m), so the student cannot pattern-match a label and must chain two relationships; the key handles that honestly -- 'not one of the named pairs, so chain two that are: <b and <f correspond ... and <f and <e form a linear pair' -- and its manual note accepts either valid chain while rejecting 'they looked supplementary'.
The manual note on problem 10 supplies a self-check a student can run alone: assuming congruence gives 6x = 20 and a non-integer x, 'which is itself a signal that the wrong rule was chosen'.
Problem 6 is the only two-step item and the key says so plainly -- 'There is no single named pair joining <f to <a, so go through <d' -- rather than inventing a name for the pair.

One shared, value-free diagram serves all ten problems with the caption 'No measures are shown here -- use the values given in each problem, and do not read anything off the drawing. (Not to scale.)', which removes the usual failure mode where a labelled figure contradicts a problem's givens.

The one-known/two-asked design of problems 1, 2, 4 and 6 deliberately pairs one congruent partner with one supplementary partner in each item, so a student applying a single habit gets exactly half of each problem wrong.
case_summary: A clean ACCEPT that survives an independent reconstruction of the geometry: I derived the eight angle positions from the TikZ coordinates in worksheet.tex and confirmed every relationship the worksheet, key and study guide name, plus all twenty machine values (62/118, 133/47, 17/61, 125/55, 12/69, 108/72, 16/76, 22/102, 15/64, 14/122) and the three declared traps (stopping at x twice, and setting a same-side interior pair equal for x=2/20). Coverage is right too: every printed answer blank has a verify entry, and the one genuinely open response -- problem 10's written justification -- is the file's single manual item, matching the judge's count. I specifically checked the closest thing to a coverage gap, the direction 'Name the relationship you used beside each answer', and did not raise it: it is a study-habit instruction in the directions rather than a per-problem response slot, and the key names the governing relationship in step 1 of all ten solutions, so a grader has the standard in hand. No defect found; root causes and improvements are deliberately empty.
